Senses.Explanation: “Bah!” is a sharp voiced exclamation recorded as rebuke, interruption, or closing cry, often immediately before a blow or descent from the seat. An abrupt exclamation, conventionally rendered “Bah!” In the Chan record it is a spoken action: named Chan speakers insert it before a rebuke, use it alone as an answer, or direct it at a named interlocutor. The Stove-Breaker strikes the stove and says “Bah! This stove is only made of mud and tiles” ; Danyuan says “Bah! Foolish fellow! Who is in the well?” ; and one record answers “What is the Way?” simply with the exclamation before ordering the unnamed questioner away. Its Chan deviation is this regular placement inside encounter dialogue as an answer or verbal blow, rather than merely narrative punctuation. The corpus gives the sound no further lexical gloss.

Senses.Explanation: A ‘good and knowledgeable person’ is a guide whom practitioners approach, recognize, or are warned to distinguish from a deceptive guide. In Chan records the role is relational: the person directs, tests, or clarifies for someone else. The term occurs 2,832 times in 311 allowlisted texts. Dahui directly says, “those called good teachers guide all beings and cause them to see nature” (夫稱善知識者，引導一切眾生，令見佛性), then describes observing people's capacities and giving teaching as medicine matches illness. He calls such reception and guidance “the proper work a good teacher ought to do” (善知識本分合做底事), and elsewhere mentions “a good teacher's eye for distinguishing people” (善知識辨人眼). The Five Lamps Compendium describes travelling people “visiting good teachers” (參善知識). Another narrative has a student say, “a great good teacher is hard to encounter even across ages; now that I have met one, why begrudge body or life?” (大善知識歷劫難逢，今既得遇，豈惜身命). Asked “what is a good teacher?” (如何是善知識), Fohai replies that lanterns, pillars, cats, and dogs are all called good teachers. The same label supplies the vocative “Good friends!” when speakers address assemblies. Direct address changes who is being hailed, not the lexical kind of label.

Senses.Note: Vocative use: Huineng or Huiyue hails the listening assembly as (善知識). This does not make the listeners their teachers.

Senses.Explanation: Sudhana is the repeatedly travelling visitor invoked from his meetings with many guides. The mysterious or profound purport: a hidden or difficult-to-reach gist that is asked about, sought, recognized, or awakened to. The records do not replace it with one stable explanatory proposition. An unnamed monk asks Guizong Zhichang what it is; after saying that no one can understand it and that directing oneself toward it departs from it, Guizong asks, "Who is seeking the mysterious purport?" Other questioners receive deliberately different replies from Zhaozhou Congshen and Zhangyi Daoqin. Jiashan Shanhui gives a reciprocal formulation in which the interlocutor's mysterious purport is Jiashan's tongue and Jiashan's is the interlocutor's tongue. A verse attributed to Sengcan warns that failing to recognize it makes quieting thoughts futile, while a lamp biography says Zhongshan Tancui greatly awakened to it. The Zen bend is the public question itself: this purport is repeatedly demanded from a named respondent, yet the recorded answers redirect the demand rather than reducing it to a portable statement.
Senses.Note: The frozen allowlisted corpus has 662 exact hits in 181 files representing 178 works. Seven exact anchors cover three public questions, Guizong Zhichang's own return question, Jiashan Shanhui's reciprocal formulation, a verse warning, and a biographical awakening. Different answers and grammatical roles remain deployments of one sought purport, not separate master-specific senses.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs join “hidden” or “subtle” with a trigger, pivot, or working. Chan records use the compound for workings disclosed in sayings, gestures, and exchanges. One verse calls them “subtle workings and marvelous function” and immediately lists raising the whisk, lifting the eyebrows, and answering questions. Another stock line says that “subtle workings beyond the norms” seek one who knows; a verse warns that people who try to grasp what precedes the working violate it beneath the phrase. The corpus can also negate it: “the intent cuts off subtle workings” stands beside “the myriad things do not arise.”

A named Caodong road or course: the first graph qualifies the road as dark, hidden, or mysterious, without establishing a physically dark roadway. The allowlisted corpus records 268 occurrences across 116 texts. Dongshan Liangjie himself names it as one of his Three Roads: ‘I have three roads for receiving people: bird course, hidden road, extending the hands’ (我有三路接人，鳥道玄路展手). The compound then moves through independently attributable teaching-seat uses rather than one fixed explanation. Fenyang Shanzhao asks his assembly, ‘What is the hidden road? Is there anyone who understands? Tell Fenyang’ (作麼生是玄路／與汾陽說看). Hongzhi Zhengjue says, ‘One step secretly shifted, the hidden road turns; the whole body released, the aeon-vessel is empty’ (一步密移玄路轉，全身放下劫壺空). Xisou Shaotan puts it at the grass tips—‘penetrate the hidden road’—while Xueguan Zhiyin says a spirit horse may gallop and a numinous crane soar, ‘crossing the hidden road freely, without touching the bird course’ (玄路縱橫，不觸鳥道). Touzi Yiqing says that even after host and guest and spoken question and answer have been established, raising the hidden road from the side is still only halfway (問答言陳，仍玄路旁提為唱／猶在半途). Shanfeng Xian turns it into teaching-hall action: ‘Holding the white staff crosswise, open the hidden road’ (橫拈白棒開玄路). The longer golden-lock family is locally explicit rather than a gloss of the bare road: Caoshan Benji says ordinary feelings and holy views are ‘the golden-lock hidden road’ and must be interchanged, while Yongjue Yuanxian calls exhaustion without the ability to turn the same compound. The Chan bend is therefore the conversion of a hidden or mysterious road into a named Caodong category that can receive, turn, be penetrated, be crossed, be opened, be appraised as halfway, and enter the golden-lock compound. None of those predicates makes it a physically dark roadway or licenses replacing every occurrence with ‘the Way.’
Senses.Note: The English road/path/way/route forms are retrieval aliases for one attested road-or-course sense, not a display menu and not a global equation between every occurrence of the graph for road and the English phrase ‘the Way.’ Five earlier rows were removed because the headword occurred in an anonymous monk's question or report while the named master only answered or examined it. Senses.Explanation: The hidden barrier is a gate to be opened, penetrated, or locked, and it appears in interview questions and barrier imagery across the records. The expression occurs 593 times in 212 allowlisted texts. One penetrates, passes, strikes, breaks, or kicks it down. Speakers ask about ‘the higher hidden barrier,’ call for one who has passed it, and ask publicly how it is passed. One discourse warns that ‘clinging to the hidden barrier’ loses the larger function; another says those not through it often construe Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing merely as facing a wall. Zen bends the gate into a public-interview checkpoint, but no corpus-wide sentence defines fixed content behind it.

Senses.Explanation: “do you yet understand?” In Chan records it is a recurring public-interview question after the identified master has spoken, displayed an object, stood up, or made another gesture. The addressee may answer “I do not understand”; the identified master may then speak again, request an object, or close the address. In hall discourse it also turns from an exposition to the assembly: “Do you get it? If not yet…” A long pause, a verse, a staff gesture, or the closing “take care” is frequently recorded after the question. The distinctive Chan deployment is therefore not a private report of comprehension but an observable demand made to an emperor, official, monk, or whole assembly in a recorded encounter.
